e.t: Angel is the word used for an angel; in the plural, it refers to angels. It names a distinct kind of being spoken of throughout the Greek New Testament, rather than an action, quality, or place. The word appears 175 times in 171 verses in this corpus, from Matthew through Revelation, showing that angels are a recurring part of New Testament language. Its exact role depends on the surrounding verse.

Purity means cleanness or freedom from corruption. This noun describes a condition of being pure, especially as a quality expected in conduct. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Timothy, and both occurrences are rendered “purity.” Its exact emphasis in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to purity as a quality to be maintained.

“Amen” is a word that affirms something as certain, true, or firmly established. It can express agreement with what has been said and is also used as a concluding affirmation. In the Greek New Testament, it appears 128 times, from Matthew through Revelation, showing that it is a recurring word of certainty and affirmation rather than a description of an object or action. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on how it functions within the surrounding sentence.

Antioch is the name of a city mentioned in the Greek New Testament. The word functions as a proper place-name rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. It appears 18 times in 17 New Testament verses, mostly in Acts, where Antioch is an important setting in the early spread of the gospel. It also appears in Galatians and 2 Timothy. The name itself identifies the location; its particular significance in any verse comes from the surrounding passage.

e.t: This word means to consider someone or something worthy, or to deem it deserving of a certain recognition or response. It expresses an evaluation: a person or thing is regarded as having the appropriate worth for what is being considered. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times in seven verses, including passages rendered with the idea of being worthy. Its precise force depends on what or whom the sentence evaluates, but its central sense remains the judgment that someone or something merits a particular regard.

This word refers to lambs—young sheep. It names the animal itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 10:3, and its ordinary meaning is clear from the direct gloss “lambs.” Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word’s basic sense remains the same: young sheep. This word means “unstable,” describing someone who lacks firmness or steadiness. It is used as an adjective, so it characterizes people rather than naming an action. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, both times in 2 Peter, where the English rendering is “unstable.” Its basic sense is a person who is not securely settled and may therefore be easily shaken or influenced. The surrounding verse supplies the particular reason for that instability; the word itself identifies the person’s lack of steadiness.

This word refers to a palace or something royal. It describes a place or setting associated with a king and his court, rather than an ordinary home or public building. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 7:25. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s exact role in that sentence cannot be described further; its basic sense remains a palace or royal place. The related idea of royalty helps readers recognize that the word points to kingly surroundings and status.

This word refers to fine linen, a high-quality fabric made from linen fibers. It describes a material valued for its fineness and suitability for clothing or other garments. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, all in Revelation, where it is associated with garments and cloth. Its basic meaning remains focused on the material itself rather than on a person, action, or spiritual quality.

Gomorrah is a proper name referring to the place called Gomorrah. In the Greek New Testament, it appears four times, each in a different verse: Matthew 10:15, Romans 9:29, 2 Peter 2:6, and Jude 1:7. The word identifies a specific place rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word means “denarius,” the name of a money coin. In the Greek New Testament, it refers to a specific unit of currency used in accounts of payment, wages, debts, and money shown to Jesus. It occurs 16 times in 15 verses, from Matthew through Revelation, so its basic meaning remains consistent wherever it appears. The surrounding verse determines how the coin functions in that particular statement.

Dionysius is a personal name, referring to a man rather than describing a quality, action, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Acts 17:34. The name itself identifies the individual; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand his particular role there. It should therefore be read as a proper name preserved in English as “Dionysius,” not as a general word with a broader abstract meaning.

The word means “least”: it marks a person or thing as the lowest or smallest when compared with others. It functions as a comparative description, pointing to what has the least standing, extent, or measure within a group. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 14 times, including uses rendered “least” in Matthew, Luke, and other New Testament books. Its exact force in a verse depends on what is being compared.

e.t: This word means “to oppose”: to stand against someone or something rather than support or yield to it. It functions as a verb, describing active resistance or opposition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Mark 6:19, Luke 11:53, and Galatians 5:1. The precise force of the opposition in each passage depends on its surrounding context, but the central idea remains standing against or resisting.

e.t: This word describes acting “in a godly manner” or “piously”—with conduct directed toward reverence for God. It functions as an adverb, telling how a person behaves rather than naming the person or the action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs two times, in 2 Timothy and Titus. Its precise force in either verse is understood from the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning is behavior marked by devotion to God.

This word means “priesthood” or “priestly office,” referring to the recognized role or service of a priest. It describes priestly responsibility as an established position rather than merely a single act of worship. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs two times, in Luke and Hebrews. Its precise emphasis in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence and subject, but its central idea remains the priestly office or the priesthood itself.

This word means “lower,” describing something positioned below another place or level. It functions as a comparative description, drawing attention to relative position rather than naming a specific object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Ephesians 4:9. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea remains the description of something lower in position.

This word means “heat,” referring to warmth or high temperature. It functions as a noun, naming heat as a physical condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, and each occurrence is rendered “heat,” confirming this straightforward sense. Its references span Matthew, Luke, and James, so the word appears in more than one kind of passage while retaining the same basic meaning. The surrounding verse determines what effect or comparison the heat has in each case.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, in two verses: Matthew 24:22 and Mark 13:20. Its basic sense remains the same in each occurrence, while the surrounding verse determines what is being shortened. It expresses an action, not a person, object, or abstract quality.

e.t: This word means to learn, to come to understand something, or to gain knowledge. It describes the process of receiving and recognizing instruction, information, or a lesson. Depending on the sentence, it can refer either to an ongoing act of learning or to knowledge that someone has already gained. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 25 times, showing that learning is a recurring biblical activity rather than a rare idea. Its use spans the Gospels, Acts, the letters, and Revelation.

This word refers to a musician—someone who makes or performs music. It is a noun naming a person associated with musical performance, rather than describing a song, instrument, or musical style. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 18:22. Because no verse text is provided here, the word’s precise role in that sentence must be understood from its surrounding context, but its ordinary meaning is a musician or musical performer.

This word means “dwelling,” referring to a place where someone lives or stays. It describes a residence rather than the person who occupies it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in 2 Corinthians 5:2 and Jude 1:6. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a dwelling or habitation. The word therefore points readers to the place associated with living, remaining, or being housed.

This word refers to a huge millstone, specifically one worked by a donkey. It describes the large, heavy stone used for grinding grain, rather than the smaller hand millstone a person could turn. In the Greek New Testament, it appears only twice, in Matthew 18:6 and Mark 9:42. Both references identify the same kind of exceptionally heavy millstone. The word’s central sense is therefore concrete and specific: a donkey-driven millstone, used as a picture of great weight and severity when the surrounding verse applies it.

e.t: This word means “to trap”—to try to catch or ensnare someone, often by placing them in a difficult position. It is a verb describing an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 22:15. The word itself identifies the intent to trap; the surrounding passage is needed to explain who was targeted and how the attempt was made. Its central idea remains an effort to catch someone through a snare or challenging situation.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to follow” or “have followed.” It describes going after someone or something, or continuing along the same course. The basic idea is sustained following rather than a brief or isolated action. It occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, each in a different verse, so its precise emphasis depends on the sentence where it appears. In ordinary reading, it points to following a person, teaching, example, or course of action.

e.t: This word means “to pass by” or “to pass through,” describing movement from one place or point to another. It is used of people moving along a route, past something, or through an area. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, all in Matthew and Mark, and its basic sense remains focused on going onward rather than stopping. The exact force in any verse depends on what the person or group is passing and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek New Testament word means “spirit” and can also refer to “breath” or “wind.” It describes an unseen force or presence, whether spoken of as a spirit, spirits, the Spirit, breath, or wind. In the New Testament it occurs 379 times, so its precise sense depends on how it functions in each sentence. It is especially common in Acts, 1 Corinthians, Luke, Romans, and Revelation. The word appears from Matthew through Revelation, including passages that speak of the Spirit and of spirits.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs two times, so its basic meaning is narrowly and consistently represented. The surrounding words determine who goes before and what purpose that movement serves in each passage.

e.t: This word means “to spit,” describing the act of ejecting saliva from the mouth. It is a concrete action word rather than a broad description of healing, cleansing, or another spiritual idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in the Gospels. Its recorded uses appear in Mark twice and John once, but the word itself retains the straightforward meaning of spitting. The surrounding verse and passage determine why that action occurs in each instance.

The word means “groan” or “groaning,” referring to the expression of a burden or deep distress. It can describe groaning itself or groanings expressed by someone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Acts 7:34 and Romans 8:26. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central sense remains a deeply felt groan or expression of distress.

e.t: This word means “to embrace” or “to put one's arms around” someone. It describes the physical act of taking a person into one's arms, expressing close contact and personal care. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 20:10. Because the word itself names an embracing action rather than a broad idea, its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative. Its central meaning remains the same: drawing someone close by embracing them.

e.t: This word means “quick” or “quickly,” describing something that happens with speed. It marks an action as immediate or swift rather than slow or delayed. In the Greek New Testament, it carries this straightforward sense across nine occurrences, including commands, movements, and warnings. Its exact force in any verse depends on the action it describes, but its central idea remains speed and promptness.

Tryphena is a personal name, referring to a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Romans 16:12, and is rendered as the name “Tryphena.” Because it is a name, its ordinary function is to identify someone; the surrounding verse and passage provide any further significance for that mention. The name itself does not express a general spiritual quality or instruction.

This word means “donkey,” referring to the familiar domesticated riding or working animal. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, so it is a specific animal term rather than a broad word for livestock or transportation. Its exact significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains clear: a donkey. The word appears in Matthew 21:5 and 2 Peter 2:16.

e.t: This word means “Chaldean,” a name identifying a person belonging to the Chaldean people. It functions as a people-name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 7:4. The word itself identifies the people being referred to, while the surrounding verse and passage determine its precise role in that statement.

This word means a proclamation, specifically a proclamation from God. It refers to a message or declaration presented as coming from God rather than merely expressing a human opinion. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Romans 11:4. Its basic meaning identifies the source and character of the announcement; the surrounding verse and passage determine the specific force of that proclamation there.
